act_name: Consumer Protection Act, 2019
heading: Definition of Consumer
content: A consumer is any person who buys goods or hires any service for a consideration which has been paid or promised or partly paid. It includes offline and online transactions, electronic means, teleshopping, direct selling, or multi-level marketing. It does not include a person who obtains goods for resale or commercial purpose.

act_name: Consumer Protection Act, 2019
heading: Consumer Rights
content: Consumers have six core rights: (i) Right to be protected against marketing of hazardous goods; (ii) Right to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard, and price of goods or services; (iii) Right to be assured of access to a variety of goods or services at competitive prices; (iv) Right to be heard and represented in consumer forums; (v) Right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices or restrictive trade practices; (vi) Right to consumer awareness.

heading: Deficiency in Service
content: Deficiency means any fault, imperfection, shortcoming, or inadequacy in the quality, nature, and manner of performance that is required to be maintained by law or contract. It includes act of negligence, omission, or deliberate withholding of relevant information.

heading: Pecuniary Jurisdiction of Consumer Commissions

act_name: Consumer Protection Act, 2019
heading: Manner of Filing Complaint and E-Daakhil
content: A complaint can be filed by a consumer, registered consumer association, or Central/State Government. Complaints can be filed in the District Commission within whose local limits the complainant resides or personally works for gain, or where the opposite party resides. Complaints can also be filed electronically via the E-Daakhil portal (edaakhil.nic.in) without needing an advocate.

act_name: Indian Contract Act, 1872 & Legal Notice Basics
category: Basic Legal Procedures and Legal Aid
heading: Essential Elements of Valid Contract
content: An agreement enforceable by law is a contract. All agreements are contracts if they are made by free consent of parties competent to contract, for a lawful consideration, with a lawful object, and not expressly declared void. Written agreements, stamped as per State Stamp Acts, carry strong evidentiary value under the Indian Evidence Act.

act_name: Indian Contract Act, 1872 & Legal Notice Basics
category: Basic Legal Procedures and Legal Aid
heading: Compensation for Breach of Contract
content: When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things. If a sum is named in the contract as penalty or liquidated damages, the party complaining is entitled to receive reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount named.

act_name: Indian Contract Act, 1872 & Legal Notice Basics
category: Basic Legal Procedures and Legal Aid
heading: Understanding and Responding to Legal Notices
content: A legal notice is a formal written document sent by an aggrieved party giving the other party an opportunity to rectify a grievance or settle a dispute within a stipulated period (usually 15 to 30 days) before initiating litigation. Key rules: (1) Never ignore a legal notice; silence can be portrayed in court as admission of facts; (2) Check the date of receipt and retain the envelope/tracking proof; (3) Verify claims against signed agreements and bank statements; (4) Reply with factual rebuttal drafted clearly or through an advocate; (5) If claims are true, explore amicable settlement.

category: Basic Legal Procedures and Legal Aid
heading: Period of Limitation for Civil & Money Recovery
content: Under the Limitation Act 1963, the time limit to file a suit for recovery of money or breach of contract is generally 3 years from the date when the right to sue accrues (e.g. from the date the payment became due or breach occurred). Filing after 3 years is barred by limitation unless there was written acknowledgment of debt within the limitation period.

act_name: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 & NALSA Guidelines
category: Basic Legal Procedures and Legal Aid
heading: Criteria for Entitlement to Free Legal Services
content: Every person who has to file or defend a case is entitled to free legal services if that person is: (a) a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe; (b) a victim of trafficking in human beings or beggar; (c) a woman or a child; (d) a person with disability as defined in PwD Act; (e) a person under circumstances of underserved want such as victim of mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster; (f) an industrial workman; (g) in custody in a protective home or psychiatric hospital; (h) in receipt of annual income less than statutory threshold prescribed by State Govt (ranging between Rs. 1 Lakh to Rs. 3 Lakhs per annum across states, Rs. 5 Lakhs before Supreme Court Legal Services Committee).

act_name: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 & NALSA Guidelines
category: Basic Legal Procedures and Legal Aid
heading: Lok Adalats & Permanent Lok Adalats
content: Lok Adalats are alternative dispute resolution forums where disputes/cases pending in the court of law or at pre-litigation stage are settled amicably. An award made by Lok Adalats is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final and binding on all the parties. No appeal lies to any court against the award. No court fee is charged, and if a case already pending in court is settled in Lok Adalat, court fee already paid is refunded.

act_name: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 & Code on Wages, 2019
heading: Time of Payment of Wages
content: Every person responsible for the payment of wages shall fix wage-periods not exceeding one month. Where less than 1,000 persons are employed, wages must be paid before the expiry of the 7th day after the last day of the wage period. In other establishments, before the expiry of the 10th day. Where employment is terminated by the employer, wages earned must be paid before the expiry of the second working day from termination.

act_name: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 & Code on Wages, 2019
heading: Permissible Deductions Only
content: Wages must be paid to every employee without unauthorized deductions of any kind except those specified under Section 7 (such as authorized fines, absence from duty, damage to goods expressly entrusted, house accommodation provided by employer, income tax, provident fund). Arbitrary withholding of earned salary as penalty or notice-pay forfeiture beyond contractual limits is illegal.

act_name: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 & Code on Wages, 2019
heading: Eligibility for Gratuity
content: Gratuity is payable to an employee on the termination of employment after rendering continuous service for not less than five years: (a) on superannuation, (b) on retirement or resignation, or (c) on death or disablement (five-year condition does not apply in case of death or disablement). Maximum tax-free limit is Rs. 20 Lakhs.

act_name: Payment of Wages Act, 1936 & Code on Wages, 2019
heading: Recommended Steps for Unpaid Salary
content: 1. Send a formal Demand Email detailing unpaid salary months, calculation, and bank records. 2. If unpaid within 7-15 days, send a formal Legal Notice through an advocate or self-drafted under registered post. 3. File a complaint before the District Labour Officer / Assistant Labour Commissioner for conciliation. 4. If unresolved, file an application under Section 15 of Payment of Wages Act or Section 33C(2) of Industrial Disputes Act, or a summary suit in Civil Court under Order 37 CPC.

heading: Mandatory Written Tenancy Agreement
content: No person shall let or take on rent any premises except by an agreement in writing, which must be jointly informed to the Rent Authority within a period of two months from the date of execution. Verbal tenancy arrangements have no statutory backing for eviction or dispute enforcement.

act_name: Model Tenancy Act, 2021 and State Rent Control Frameworks
heading: Security Deposit Limits & Return
content: Security deposit to be paid by the tenant in advance shall not exceed two months' rent in case of residential premises, and a maximum of six months' rent in case of non-residential premises. The security deposit shall be refunded to the tenant by the landlord at the time of taking vacant possession of the premises, after making due deduction of any liability relating to arrears of rent and unpaid utility charges.

act_name: Model Tenancy Act, 2021 and State Rent Control Frameworks
heading: Revision of Rent
content: Revision of rent shall be in terms of the written tenancy agreement. The landlord must give written notice to the tenant three months before the enhanced rent becomes payable. If the tenant does not give notice of termination before the expiry of notice, tenant is deemed to have accepted the revision.

heading: Prohibition of Essential Services Cutoff
content: No landlord or property manager shall, either by himself or through any person, cut off or withhold any essential supply or service (such as water, electricity, passage, sanitation, lift) in the premises occupied by the tenant, even in case of non-payment of rent. Doing so is an offense punishable by penalties from the Rent Authority.

act_name: Model Tenancy Act, 2021 and State Rent Control Frameworks
heading: Protection from Arbitrary Eviction & Notice
content: A landlord cannot forcibly evict a tenant without approaching the Rent Authority / Rent Court and obtaining an eviction order. Valid grounds for eviction include failure to pay rent for two consecutive months after statutory demand notice, unauthorized subletting, causing substantial structural damage, or bona fide personal need. Self-help eviction (changing locks, throwing out belongings) is illegal.

heading: Steps for Withheld Security Deposit
content: 1. Send a formal written Demand Letter or Legal Notice via registered post with acknowledgment due (RPAD) giving 15 days to refund the balance deposit. 2. If landlord fails to pay, file an application before the Rent Authority/Rent Court under the State Tenancy Act or file a consumer complaint under Consumer Protection Act (if landlord is a commercial housing provider/coliving/PG) or a summary recovery suit under Order 37 CPC.
